column3: Graph Neural Network-Based Anomaly Detection in Multivariate Time Series
column4: Ailin Deng, Bryan Hooi
column6: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-21)
column8: Detecting faults and attacks in sensor data is hard because there are many sensors and they affect each other. The authors learn a graph of how sensors relate, use a graph neural network to forecast each sensor, and use attention weights to explain alarms; tested on two real sensor datasets with known attacks (SWaT and WADI). It finds anomalies more accurately than baselines and helps users locate the root-cause sensor.
column9: Widely used baseline (GDN) tested on SWaT and WADI; its attention weights point to the sensor behind each alarm. Public code.

column3: Federated Learning-Based Explainable Anomaly Detection for Industrial Control Systems
column4: Truong Thu Huong, Ta Phuong Bac, Kieu Ngan Ha, Nguyen Viet Hoang, Nguyen Xuan Hoang, Nguyen Tai Hung
column8: Smart factories need anomaly detection for industrial control systems that is accurate, quick to retrain and light enough for edge devices, and most solutions cannot explain their alarms. FedeX combines a variational autoencoder, federated learning across factory zones, SVDD for automatic thresholds and Kernel SHAP explanations; tested on a SCADA liquid-storage dataset and SWaT, on Raspberry Pi 4 edge devices. It beats 14 other methods (recall 1, F1 0.9857 on SWaT), trains in about 7.5 minutes and uses about 14% memory. (From the IEEE Xplore page you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: Moved up from extras - IEEE Access, a weaker venue. Kernel SHAP for ICS (SCADA liquid storage + SWaT) on Raspberry Pi 4 edge devices. It measures the cost of training on the edge and recommends running SHAP only periodically (e.g. once a week) - support for your gap.

column3: GRU-Based Interpretable Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control System
column4: Chaofan Tang, Lijuan Xu, Bo Yang, Yongwei Tang, Dawei Zhao
column8: Anomaly detection for industrial control systems needs good accuracy, interpretability and fast training at the same time. The authors propose GRN, which combines a graph neural network (to learn how sensors relate) with GRUs (to learn short- and long-term time patterns), tested on the SWaT and WADI water-treatment datasets against nine methods. GRN gives better precision and recall and is more interpretable than GDN (no exact numbers in the abstract).
column9: Interpretable detector built for industrial control systems, tested on SWaT and WADI, in Computers & Security. Free to read.

column3: Explainable Anomaly Detection for Industrial Control System Cybersecurity
column4: Do Thu Ha, Nguyen Xuan Hoang, Nguyen Viet Hoang, Nguyen Huu Du, Truong Thu Huong, Kim Phuc Tran
column8: Industrial control systems run factories and utilities, and AI anomaly detectors that protect them perform well but are hard to interpret. The authors use explainable AI (Gradient SHAP) to make an LSTM-autoencoder + one-class SVM detector more reliable and understandable, tested on a well-known SCADA gas-pipeline dataset. They show the method works on that dataset (no numbers in the abstract).
column9: Moved up from extras - conference proceedings (IFAC), a weaker venue. Gradient SHAP explains an LSTM-autoencoder + one-class SVM detector on SCADA gas-pipeline data. 104 citations.

column3: An Explainable and Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Model for Threat Detection in Cyber-Physical-Social Systems
column4: Abbas Yazdinejad, Zahra Dehghani Mohammadabadi, Ali Dehghantanha, Gautam Srivastava
column6: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems
column8: Cyber-physical-social systems (energy, transport) are exposed to cyberattacks, and current detectors often ignore privacy, explainability and reliability. The authors build a federated-learning threat detector that protects data with differential privacy and Paillier homomorphic encryption and explains alarms with SHAP; tested on SWaT, Gas Pipeline and UNSW-NB15. It reaches 97.46%, 98.85% and 93.60% accuracy on those datasets and beats several baselines.
column9: SHAP explanations on real ICS datasets (SWaT, Gas Pipeline), plus privacy protection (federated learning).

column3: Explainable correlation-based anomaly detection for Industrial Control Systems
column4: E. Birihanu, I. Lendak
column8: (From our check of the Frontiers page on 11 Oct.) A correlation-based anomaly detector for industrial control systems - an LSTM autoencoder whose alarms are explained with SHAP - tested on SWaT, HIL-HAI and an IoT Modbus dataset.
column9: Moved up from extras - Frontiers in AI, a weaker venue. SHAP explains an LSTM-autoencoder ICS detector on SWaT and HAI. Public code (repository opened and checked).

column3: An explainable unsupervised anomaly detection framework for Industrial Internet of Things
column4: Yilixiati Abudurexiti, Guangjie Han, Fan Zhang, Li Liu
column8: Industrial IoT anomaly detection is hard because labelled attack data is scarce and most detectors cannot explain themselves. The authors propose an unsupervised framework (CCTAK): a CNN with attention finds local patterns in sensor time series, and a VAE built on an improved TCN and KAN captures long-term patterns; SHAP explains which features drive each anomaly. It beats other unsupervised methods (no numbers in the abstract; the article lists four datasets including SWaT and SKAB). (From the ScienceDirect abstract you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: Unsupervised (no attack labels needed) with SHAP explanations; uses real industrial sensor data, including SWaT. Published in Computers & Security.

column3: Attributions for ML-based ICS Anomaly Detection: From Theory to Practice
column4: Clement Fung, Eric Zeng, Lujo Bauer
column6: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS 2024)
column8: ML anomaly detectors can flag attacks on industrial control systems (power, water plants) but do not say which sensor or actuator was attacked, so finding the root cause is hard. The authors compare state-of-the-art attribution methods (which name the features behind an alarm) on real attacks from several ICS datasets. The methods work worse than earlier papers suggested, especially at the moment of detection and for on/off actuators, but combining several methods (ensembles) helps.
column9: READ FIRST. Compares attribution (explanation) methods on real attacks from several ICS datasets and finds they work worse than earlier papers suggested, especially at the moment of detection. Public code - a ready-made starting point.

column3: Data-centric explainable artificial intelligence techniques for cyber-attack detection in microgrid networks
column4: Rohit Trivedi, Sandipan Patra, Shafi Khadem
column8: Machine-learning attack detectors need clean, well-prepared data and careful tuning, and their decisions are hard to interpret. The authors propose a three-stage framework that uses SHAP to explain the model, applied to cyber-attack detection in a simulated CIGRE low-voltage microgrid, with SMOTE+ENN data balancing, Boruta feature selection and TPE hyperparameter tuning. Prediction improves at each stage (no numbers given in the abstract).
column9: Cyber-attack detection in a simulated microgrid (CIGRE low-voltage), explained with SHAP.

column3: WaXAI: Explainable Anomaly Detection in Industrial Control Systems and Water Systems
column4: Kornkamon Mathuros, Sarad Venugopalan, Sridhar Adepu
column6: Proceedings of the 10th ACM Cyber-Physical System Security Workshop (CPSS 2024)
column8: Industrial control systems mostly run without human supervision, and ML detectors for them need long training and cannot say which component is anomalous. The authors train two recent detectors (ECOD and DeepSVDD) on data from the SWaT water-treatment testbed, apply explainable-AI models to show why the detectors decide as they do, and measure how good those explanations are. Both detectors need shorter training and detection times with comparable detection rates (the abstract does not name the XAI methods).
column9: Moved up from extras - workshop paper (ACM CPSS 2024, University of Bristol), a weaker venue. Explains two ICS detectors (ECOD, DeepSVDD) on SWaT and measures how good the explanations are; also reports training and detection times.

column3: Explainable Intrusion Detection in Industrial Control Systems
column4: Reham Eltomy, Wassila Lalouani
column6: 2024 IEEE 7th International Conference on Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems (ICPS)
column8: Intrusion detectors for industrial control systems often act as black boxes and miss zero-day attacks. The authors build a multi-head-attention model plus a new autoencoder to classify ICS network traffic and catch zero-day attacks, and use the attention weights to explain each decision; tested on water-system ICS testbeds. It infers zero-day attacks with over 89% accuracy while giving interpretable results. (From the IEEE abstract you pasted on 11 Oct.)
column9: Moved up from extras - conference paper (IEEE ICPS 2024), a weaker venue. ICS intrusion detection on water-system testbeds, explained with attention weights instead of SHAP; focuses on zero-day attacks.

column3: Investigation of the Robustness of XAI-Based Federated Learning Against Adversarial Attacks for Smart Grid False Data Detection
column4: Islam Elgarhy, Mahmoud M. Badr, Mohamed M. E. A. Mahmoud, Jianbing Ni, Maazen Alsabaan, Tariq A. Alshawi
column8: Federated learning can detect false data in smart power grids while keeping consumer data private, but these detectors can be fooled by adversarial attacks during training and use. The authors test an XAI-based federated false-data detector against gradient-inversion and evasion attacks, then build a secure detector that uses the explanations to mask model gradients and to separate normal from malicious data (energy-consumption data). Using explanations cut evasion-attack success from 94.99% to 29.11% (0% with adversarial training) and raised gradient-inversion error from 0.01 to 2.60.
column9: Smart-grid false-data detection where explanations are both a target for attackers and a tool for defence.

column3: Abnormal Logical Representation Learning for Intrusion Detection in Industrial Control Systems
column4: Xinyu Xu, Yingxu Lai, Xiao Zhang, Xinrui Dong
column8: Current intrusion detection for industrial control systems does not cope with modern attacks: rule-based methods need heavy manual setup and deep-learning models are hard to interpret. The authors propose ALRL, a small neural network trained by knowledge distillation that can produce short, readable detection rules from what it learned; tested on two public ICS datasets. The abstract reports strong attack classification and says the rules detect all attack types (no exact numbers given).
column9: Intrusion detection for industrial control systems where the model itself produces short, readable detection rules (no SHAP needed); tested on two public ICS datasets.

column3: ShaTS: a Shapley-based explainability method for time series artificial intelligence models
column4: Manuel Franco de la Peña, Ángel Luis Perales Gómez, Lorenzo Fernández Maimó
column8: Usual explanation methods for industrial-IoT anomaly detection ignore the time order of sensor data, so explanations can be vague or hard to act on. The authors propose ShaTS, a model-agnostic Shapley-based method for time-series models that groups features in advance to keep time dependencies; tested on the SWaT water-treatment dataset. ShaTS finds the critical moments and the affected sensors, actuators and process stages, and beats SHAP in both accuracy and resource efficiency (no numbers in the abstract).
column9: READ FIRST - close to our idea. Full text (read 12 Oct): times SHAP and ShaTS per time window against a 1-second real-time limit on SWaT, with one LSTM detector, on a powerful desktop (RTX 4080 GPU). ShaTS is faster and uses less memory than SHAP. The authors say the speed-vs-accuracy trade-off of the method's settings is 'not examined'. Public code.

column3: Explainable AI for Process-Aware Attack Detection in Industrial Control Systems
column4: Léa Astrid Kenmogne, Stéphane Mocanu
column6: 2024 IEEE 10th International Conference on Network Softwarization (NetSoft)
column8: Famous ICS attacks (Stuxnet, BlackEnergy, Industroyer) followed the communication protocols, so pattern-based detectors missed them, and they targeted the physical process directly. The authors study how well an AI-based detector catches such stealthy, process-level attacks and how well its decisions can be explained. (The abstract names no dataset or numbers. From the IEEE Xplore page you pasted on 12 Oct.)
column9: Moved up from extras - conference paper (IEEE NetSoft 2024), a weaker venue. Explainable detection of stealthy, process-level ICS attacks (Stuxnet-style) that follow protocol rules. The abstract names no dataset.

column3: XAI-CPS: An explainable hybrid deep learning framework for real-time anomaly detection and adaptive threat mitigation in networked Cyber-Physical Systems
column4: Iftikhar Rasheed, Hala Mostafa, Ghulam Mohayudin
column8: Networked cyber-physical systems in critical infrastructure face multi-step attacks across layers. XAI-CPS combines a temporal-attention convolutional LSTM with graph neural networks to model sensors over time and across components, explains alarms with Layer-wise Relevance Propagation that respects physical process limits, and uses reinforcement learning to choose responses; tested on SWaT, WADI, BATADAL and a new IIoT dataset. Mean F1 is 92.9% (4.6-5.2 points above state of the art), false positives drop 37.5%, experts agreed with 89.3% of explanations, and response time falls 67% with availability above 99.2%. (From the ScienceDirect abstract you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: READ FIRST. Uses SWaT, WADI and BATADAL; physics-aware explanations (LRP) that human experts agreed with 89.3% of the time. The abstract does not say how long explanations take - check the full text.

column3: Interpretable intelligent intrusion detection systems for cybersecurity in smart digital substations
column4: Matthew Oinonen, Walid G. Morsi
column8: Securing smart digital substations is getting harder, and current intrusion detectors use black-box ML/DL models that operators cannot easily trust. The authors run what they call the first experimental comparison of several explainable-AI techniques, scoring them on explainability, trustworthiness, complexity, interpretability, stability, faithfulness and fairness, on a realistic IEC 61850 substation testbed with a parameter-level sensitivity analysis. The aim is to guide which XAI method to choose for substation IDS (no numbers in the abstract).
column9: READ FIRST - closest to our idea. Full text (read 12 Oct): compares 7 XAI methods (incl. SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM, RISE) for substation intrusion detection on explanation quality AND time per explanation (SHAP about 8 s, LIME about 7 s, simple gradients 0.05 s), with one CNN detector on one testbed, on a powerful desktop with a GPU. Finds better explanations take longer. Note: the journal calls it an 'experimental review', but it reports new experiments. Free to read.
column16: Experimental review with new experiments (journal label: Review)

column3: A Novel MMD-Critic-XAI-Based Intrusion Detection System for Cyber-Physical Microgrids
column4: Gurmaan S. Panesar, Matthew Oinonen, Walid G. Morsi
column6: IEEE Transactions on Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems
column8: Microgrids rely on internet-connected control devices with little built-in security, and ML intrusion detectors for them are black boxes that operators cannot trust. The authors turn signals into wavelet images (scalograms) for a CNN, and use MMD-Critic - an example-based XAI method that shows typical cases and exceptions - both to tune the wavelet settings and to explain decisions; it is tested in real time with an OPAL-RT simulator and a real Siemens SIPROTEC relay sending IEC 61850 GOOSE messages. MMD-Critic raises detection accuracy to 98.85% by finding the cases the CNN got wrong, and a user interface lets grid operators see why the model decided. (From the IEEE Xplore page you pasted on 12 Oct.)
column9: Microgrid intrusion detection tested in real time with real hardware (OPAL-RT simulator and a Siemens relay); explains with example cases (MMD-Critic) and an operator interface. Same research group as Oinonen.

column3: An Explainable Approach to Process-Oriented Attacks in Industrial Control Systems using SHAP and LIME
column4: Léa Astrid Kenmogne, Stéphane Mocanu
column6: IntelliSecAI 2025 - IEEE International Conference on Computational Intelligence, Security, and Artificial Intelligence (Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia)
column8: Industrial control systems run critical physical processes, and current detectors struggle with 'process-oriented' attacks that quietly change sensor and actuator states without disturbing network traffic. The authors detect such attacks with an ML model and use LIME and SHAP to explain its predictions, tested on a simulated industrial process. It gives good detection accuracy and a full explanation of each attack, while avoiding the repeated alerts that monitoring-type approaches produce (no numbers in the abstract). (From the HAL page you pasted on 12 Oct.)
column9: Moved up from extras - conference paper (IEEE IntelliSecAI 2025), a weaker venue. SHAP and LIME explain detection of stealthy, process-level ICS attacks on a simulated industrial process (not SWaT or WADI). Free under CC BY on HAL.

column3: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Resilient Intrusion Detection in IoT-Enabled Transportation Networks
column4: Ayodeji Oseni, Nour Moustafa, Gideon Creech, Nasrin Sohrabi, Andrew Strelzoff, Zahir Tari, Igor Linkov
column6: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
column8: Deep-learning intrusion detectors for connected-vehicle (IoV/IoT) networks give many false alarms and their reasoning is hard to follow. The authors build a deep-learning IDS that uses SHAP to explain each decision, tested on the ToN_IoT dataset. It reaches 99.15% accuracy and 98.83% F1-score.
column9: SHAP-based intrusion detection for connected-vehicle networks (cyber-physical, but not a factory); tested on ToN_IoT. Highly cited.

column3: A New Explainable Deep Learning Framework for Cyber Threat Discovery in Industrial IoT Networks
column4: Izhar Ahmed Khan, Nour Moustafa, Dechang Pi, Karam M. Sallam, Albert Y. Zomaya, Bentian Li
column8: Industrial IoT data can be corrupted by false-data-injection and data-poisoning attacks, so attacks must be detected and explained. The authors build an autoencoder framework mixing convolutional and recurrent networks with a two-step sliding window, plus fully connected layers to classify and explain attacks. It extracts useful attack-pattern features and beats state-of-the-art methods on several metrics.
column9: Explainable deep-learning detector for false-data-injection and data-poisoning attacks on industrial IoT data. The abstract does not name the datasets.

column3: TRUST XAI: Model-Agnostic Explanations for AI With a Case Study on IIoT Security
column4: Maede Zolanvari, Zebo Yang, Khaled M. Khan, Raj Jain, Nader Meskin
column8: AI is a 'black box', so it is rarely trusted on its own in high-risk IoT systems, and existing XAI methods struggle to be both fast and accurate on numerical data. The authors propose TRUST, a model-agnostic explanation method built on factor analysis, mutual-information ranking and multimodal Gaussian distributions, and test it on Industrial IoT security with three datasets. TRUST explains random samples with a 98% average success rate and beats LIME in performance, speed and explainability.
column9: Proposes a new explanation method (TRUST) for industrial IoT security and shows it beats LIME on speed and accuracy - another paper that compares explanation speed.

column3: Trust my IDS: An explainable AI integrated deep learning-based transparent threat detection system for industrial networks
column4: Shifa Shoukat, Tianhan Gao, Danish Javeed, Muhammad Shahid Saeed, Muhammad Adil
column8: Industrial networks face many cyber threats. The authors build XDLTDS: an LSTM autoencoder first encodes Industrial IoT data (to resist inference attacks), then an attention-based GRU classifies threats, and SHAP explains each alarm so security analysts can see why it was flagged; they also propose a software-defined-networking deployment. Tested on N-BaIoT, Edge-IIoTset and CIC-IDS2017, it beats existing frameworks (no numbers in the abstract). (From the ScienceDirect abstract you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: SHAP explains each alarm for security analysts in industrial networks; one of its three datasets (Edge-IIoTset) is industrial IoT.

column3: An explainable efficient flow-based Industrial IoT intrusion detection system
column4: Mohammed M. Alani
column8: Attacks on Industrial IoT (e.g. in power plants or refineries) are higher-risk than on home devices. The author builds E2I3DS, a machine-learning IDS that cuts the WUSTL-IIoT-2021 dataset from 48 to 11 features and explains the model with SHAP. It reaches 99.97% accuracy, 0.01% false positives, 0.04% false negatives and a detection time of 0.1517 microseconds. (From the ScienceDirect abstract you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: SHAP-explained detector on WUSTL-IIoT. It reports how fast the detector is (0.15 microseconds) but not how long SHAP takes - useful when you describe the gap. 99.97% accuracy on one dataset - check how the test data was split.
column20: No matching PDF supplied; workbook summary only

column3: Explainable and Data-Efficient Deep Learning for Enhanced Attack Detection in IIoT Ecosystem
column4: Danish Attique, Wang Hao, Ping Wang, Danish Javeed, Prabhat Kumar
column8: Industrial IoT networks face growing attacks, and deep-learning detectors are hard to trust because their decisions are opaque. The authors build a BiLSTM detector with a self-adaptive attention mechanism that works with limited training data, plus SHAP explanations; tested on CICIDS2017 and X-IIoTID. It reaches 99.92% accuracy on CICIDS2017 and 96.54% on X-IIoTID.
column9: BiLSTM with SHAP for industrial IoT when training data is limited; tested on X-IIoTID (industrial IoT) and CICIDS2017.

column3: Machine Learning Explainability for Intrusion Detection in the Industrial Internet of Things
column4: Love Allen Chijioke Ahakonye, Cosmas Ifeanyi Nwakanma, Jae-Min Lee, Dong-Seong Kim
column8: AI attack detectors for Industrial IoT are hard to trust because they are black boxes, and XAI output itself can be hard to understand. The authors apply LIME and SHAP to intrusion detectors built with several representative AI models, and score features with 'decision and confidence impact ratios'. Experiments show these explanations help experts understand and respond to IIoT intrusions (no numbers in the abstract). (From the IEEE Xplore abstract you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: Compares LIME and SHAP across several intrusion detectors for industrial IoT. Magazine article with experiments; the abstract does not name the datasets.

column3: An Explainable Deep Learning System for Cyberattack Detection in Internet of Energy Networks
column4: Makhduma F. Saiyed, Irfan Al-Anbagi, M. Shamim Hossain
column8: Smart devices and real-time analytics in Internet-of-Energy grids add cyber risk, so attack detection must be accurate and understandable. The authors build E-SHIELD, a CNN+LSTM detector for network traffic, light enough for limited hardware, with SHAP explanations and an operator dashboard; tested on WUSTL-IIoT-2021 and CICIoT-2023. It is more accurate than existing CNN, LSTM and ensemble models (no exact numbers in the abstract).
column9: Lightweight CNN+LSTM detector with SHAP and an operator dashboard for energy networks; tested on WUSTL-IIoT-2021 and CICIoT2023.

column3: E-XAI: Evaluating Black-Box Explainable AI Frameworks for Network Intrusion Detection
column4: Osvaldo Arreche, Tanish R. Guntur, Jack W. Roberts, Mustafa Abdallah
column8: Security analysts need AI intrusion detectors explained, but there was no standard way to judge explanation methods. The authors build a framework that scores SHAP and LIME on six metrics - descriptive accuracy, sparsity, stability, efficiency (time to explain), robustness and completeness - for seven AI models on three network intrusion datasets (RoEduNet-SIMARGL2021, CICIDS-2017, NSL-KDD), and release their code. SHAP generally beats LIME, but explanation time depends heavily on the model: SHAP is practical with LightGBM, random forest and DNN, and far too slow with KNN and AdaBoost. (Abstract from the IEEE Xplore page you sent on 12 Oct; timing details from the paper's text.)
column9: Moved up from extras - IEEE Access, a weaker venue, and not about CPS. READ FIRST: it measures how long SHAP and LIME take (in hours, across 7 models), plus five other quality scores. So explanation time is already measured for general network intrusion detection - your paper must be the ICS / CPS version.
column20: No matching PDF supplied; workbook summary only

column3: xNIDS: Explaining Deep Learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems for Active Intrusion Responses
column4: Feng Wei, Hongda Li, Ziming Zhao, Hongxin Hu
column8: Deep-learning network intrusion detectors are accurate, but operators hesitate to act on their alarms because wrong responses are costly; the authors blame missing explainability. They build xNIDS, which explains a detector by sampling around past inputs and capturing dependencies between structured features, then turns the explanations into defence rules; tested on four state-of-the-art deep-learning NIDS. xNIDS beats earlier explanation methods on fidelity, sparsity, completeness and stability, and produces practical defence rules and helps troubleshoot detection errors.
column9: Not about CPS. Kept because it shows how to explain deep-learning intrusion detectors and how to score explanations (fidelity, sparsity, completeness, stability) - scores your study can reuse. Public code. Top security conference.
column20: No matching PDF supplied; workbook summary only

column3: Enhancing Intrusion Detection in CPS and IIoT with Lightweight Explainable AI Models
column4: Amanda Ericson, Kyi Thar, Stefan Forsström
column6: 2025 IEEE 21st International Conference on Factory Communication Systems (WFCS)
column8: Industrial CPS and IoT make factories more efficient but also raise cyber risk, and the authors' earlier lightweight deep-learning intrusion detectors for edge devices are black boxes. They add SHAP explanations to three small models (CNN, LSTM, GCN), convert them to TensorFlow Lite and run them on a Raspberry Pi 4, using the UNSW-NB15 dataset (general network traffic, binary benign/attack). With SHAP, average time per prediction rose from 0.115 to 0.120 ms (CNN), 3.902 to 4.236 ms (LSTM) and 0.667 to 0.688 ms (GCN), with no loss of accuracy (0.937, 0.932, 0.975). (From the full paper you sent on 12 Oct.)
column9: Moved up from extras - conference paper (IEEE WFCS 2025), a weaker venue. Full text (read 12 Oct): SHAP on a Raspberry Pi 4 with small CNN, LSTM and GCN models - but only on general network traffic (UNSW-NB15), only SHAP, no check of explanation quality, and it is unclear what the 'with SHAP' time includes (their own design sends SHAP work to a bigger 'fog' computer because the edge device is too weak). The authors list LIME, Grad-CAM, more datasets and more hardware as future work - which supports your plan.

column3: Explainable hybrid intrusion detection for SCADA/ICS: a review and research agenda
column4: Heinrihs Kristians Skrodelis, Andrejs Romanovs
column8: Systematic review of 40 studies (2014-2025) on explainable hybrid intrusion detection for SCADA/ICS. It names five gaps: zero-day coverage, false-alarm control, process awareness, explanations for operators, and deployment complexity. It proposes a conceptual (untested) architecture; its 10-50 ms SHAP figure is borrowed from other papers, not measured.
column9: EXTRA - review, not original research. Reviews 40 studies on explainable intrusion detection for SCADA/ICS and names five open gaps - use it as a reading list and for the gaps.

column3: Trustworthy Adaptive AI for Real-Time Intrusion Detection in Industrial IoT Security
column4: Mohammad Al Rawajbeh, Amala Jayanthi Maria Soosai, Lakshmana Kumar Ramasamy, Firoz Khan
column8: A lightweight, self-updating intrusion detector for industrial IoT (an ensemble of online-learning models) that explains its alerts with SHAP. Tested on ToN_IoT and Bot-IoT (network traffic, no plant process data) on a Raspberry Pi 5: 96.4% accuracy, 2.1% false positives, about 35 ms detection time per sample; SHAP explanations take about 55 ms per window of 100 samples on the Pi 5 and run in the background so they do not slow detection. (From the MDPI article page, read 12 Oct.)
column9: EXTRA - found through the ShaTS 'Cited by' check (12 Oct). Not about plant data, so 'Method only'. It times SHAP on an edge device, but uses only SHAP, only network traffic, and says time limits for real control systems are 'outside the scope' - exactly the part your paper adds.
column20: No matching PDF supplied; workbook summary only

column3: Explainable Intrusion Detection Systems (X-IDS): A Survey of Current Methods, Challenges, and Opportunities
column4: Subash Neupane, Jesse Ables, William Anderson, Sudip Mittal, Shahram Rahimi, Ioana Banicescu, Maria Seale
column8: Deep-learning intrusion detectors act like black boxes, so security analysts cannot trust or improve them. This survey reviews explainable-AI methods for intrusion detection (black-box and white-box), their trade-off between accuracy and explainability, and proposes a human-in-the-loop design. It recommends defining explainability for IDS, tailoring explanations to each user, and creating metrics to evaluate explanations.
column9: EXTRA - survey, not original research. Not about CPS: the standard survey of explainable intrusion detection; it calls for metrics to judge explanations. 407 citations.
column20: No matching PDF supplied; workbook summary only
